title: What We Know We Don't Know
summary: Source list and FAQ for an empirical-software-engineering talk: code review, simple tests and sleep have evidence, TDD and language choice are mixed or null, and most beliefs remain untested.

assertions.quote: There are many things in software we believe are true but very little we know.
there's more evidence that code review reduces bugs, and the evidence shows a bigger effect
Pairing is nice, but it's not "continous code review."
Impact of a Night of Sleep Deprivation on Novice Developers Performance

verdicts.note: Classic industrial fault studies attribute the costliest defects to requirements and design, but the split depends heavily on how faults are categorised.

Of public JavaScript bugs undetectable by Flow and TypeScript, errors implementing the specification make up 78% (SpecError alone 55%), i.e. most shipped bugs are misunderstandings of what to build rather than mechanical slips; the study does not measure how damaging each class was.

assertions.quote: Simple Testing Can Prevent Most Critical Failures

verdicts.note: A study of production outages in major distributed systems found most catastrophic failures stemmed from trivially testable error-handling bugs.

Beyond Lines of Code: Do we Need More Complexity Metrics?

verdicts.note: Studies of large codebases find most complexity metrics are strongly correlated with size and add little predictive power.

On issue resolution time rather than defects, added LoC correlated only r=0.13 while the smell-based Code Health score correlated r=-0.58, so a richer metric beat raw size here; the outcome differs from the claim's and the comparison is a brief validity check.

Method length was much more strongly correlated with cyclomatic complexity than readability was, supporting the premise that size and complexity metrics largely overlap; the paper does not compare LoC and complexity as defect predictors directly.

Spearman correlations with Vista failures: size 0.75 pre-release / 0.69 post-release versus complexity 0.70 / 0.53 (Windows 7: 0.70/0.26 vs 0.56/0.37), so lines of code tracks defects at least as well as complexity.
With complexity normalised by size, size stays a significant explainer of post-release defects in two of four Qt/VTK/ITK release models while complexity is significant in none.

assertions.quote: The Influence of Organizational Structure On Software Quality: An Empirical Case Study

verdicts.note: One large industrial study found this strongly, but it has few replications outside that company.

On 3,404 Windows Vista binaries (50M+ LOC, 50 random splits), eight organizational metrics predict failure-prone binaries with 86.2% precision and 84.0% recall versus 78.6/79.9 for churn, 79.3/66.0 for complexity, 74.4/69.9 for dependencies, 83.8/54.4 for coverage and 73.8/62.9 for pre-release bugs; single system.

In Vista and Windows 7 the number of minor contributors correlated more strongly with pre- and post-release failures than any other metric Microsoft collects, and adding it to a size/churn/complexity model raised variance explained from 26% to 46% (pre-release Vista).
In Qt, VTK and ITK the ownership metrics (minor authors) add significant explanatory power to every post-release defect model, while size is significant in only two and complexity in none.
